title: Checklist: Government, Daily Life and Laws by Name
summary: Government services, everyday behaviour, environment, the main laws, and your daily safety checklist.

body.text: The final part of your checklist: government services, everyday behaviour, the environment, and the main laws you should recognise by name.
🏛️ Part 10: Government services and your rights

items: 131. RTI (Right to Information). Any citizen can ask a government office for information; they must usually reply in 30 days.
132. Voting rights. Learn voter registration, eligibility and how to vote lawfully.
133. Passport. Know the application, renewal and travel-document rules.
134. Aadhaar. Understand enrolment, correction, and the limits on when it can be demanded.
135. PAN. Know when PAN is required for tax and financial work, and how to report misuse.
136. Public grievances. Learn how to complain to a department and track the reply.
137. Government schemes. Check eligibility, how to apply, the benefits and the appeal route.
138. Certificates. Learn how to get birth, death, income and community certificates.
139. Public services. Know the procedure for utilities, municipal services and local complaints.
140. Legal aid. Approach your District Legal Services Authority for free help if you qualify.
141. Court orders. Learn how to verify an order, comply with it, and challenge it properly.
142. RTI appeals. If an RTI is refused or ignored, learn the first and second appeal steps.

body.text: 🚨 Part 11: Public behaviour and everyday offences

items: 143. Public nuisance. Do not block, endanger or seriously disturb others.
144. Noise rules. Follow the rules on loudspeakers and loud sound, especially at night.
145. Trespassing. Do not enter or stay on someone else's property without permission.
146. Assault and fighting. Physical aggression is a crime, even if it started as an argument.
147. Self-defence. Use only as much force as needed; hitting back after the danger has passed is not self-defence.
148. Threats and extortion. Threatening someone, or demanding money by threat, is an offence.
149. Damage to property. Deliberately damaging someone's property has criminal and civil consequences.
150. Alcohol and public conduct. Follow your state's rules on alcohol and public behaviour.
151. Public smoking. Learn where smoking is banned.
152. Drugs. Possession, use, supply and trafficking of drugs are serious offences.
153. Public photography. Respect privacy and rules when filming people or restricted places.
154. Peaceful protests. You have a right to peaceful assembly, with reasonable conditions.
155. Police directions. Follow lawful directions; if you believe an action is unlawful, use the proper complaint route.
156. Waste disposal. Follow local rules on littering, segregation and dumping.
157. Water and electricity. Illegal connections and meter tampering are offences.
158. Environment. There are rules against pollution, dumping and cutting trees unlawfully.
159. Animal welfare. Cruelty to animals is punishable; owners have duties too.
160. Food safety. You have protections against unsafe food, and a way to complain.
161. Public health. Follow lawful public-health directions.
162. Building and fire safety. Know the fire-safety and emergency-exit rules for buildings.
163. Community responsibilities. Respect others' rights, public property and local rules.
164. Fundamental Duties. Article 51A lists citizens' duties - respecting the Constitution, protecting public property and promoting harmony.
165. Civic participation. Raise local problems with your panchayat, municipality or the right authority.

body.text: 📘 Part 13: The main laws, by name

items: Constitution of India - fundamental rights, government powers and duties.
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - criminal offences and punishments.
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - criminal procedure, arrest, investigation and bail.
Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) - evidence in legal proceedings.
Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 - vehicles and road traffic.
Consumer Protection Act, 2019 - consumer rights and remedies.
Information Technology Act, 2000 - electronic records and cyber offences.
Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 - protection of personal data.
Right to Information Act, 2005 - access to information from public authorities.
Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 - legal aid.
Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 - domestic-violence protections.
Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013 (POSH) - workplace harassment.
POCSO Act, 2012 - protection of children from sexual offences.
Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 - dowry.
Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 - child marriage.
Income-tax Act, 1961 - income tax.
Transfer of Property Act, 1882 - property transfers.
Registration Act, 1908 - registration of documents.
Indian Contract Act, 1872 - contracts.
Hindu Succession Act, 1956 and Special Marriage Act, 1954 - succession and civil marriage.
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 - environmental protection.
Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 - food safety.
Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 - cheques and promissory notes.
Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 - care of parents and seniors.
Carry the vehicle documents you need for your journey.
Follow traffic signals, speed limits and helmet or seat-belt rules.
Never share OTPs, UPI PINs or passwords.
Read loan agreements, contracts and important documents before signing.
Keep receipts, salary records, agreements and important messages.
Verify official calls, notices, challans and payment requests.
Report online financial fraud immediately.
Never ignore a court summons or lawful official notice.
Respect privacy, and never threaten, assault or harass anyone.
Know how to reach legal aid and emergency services.
indiacode.nic.in - read the actual Acts.
sci.gov.in - the Constitution and the Supreme Court.
mha.gov.in - criminal-law information.
nalsa.gov.in - free legal aid.
rbi.org.in - banking rules and complaints.
tn.gov.in - Tamil Nadu government services.

body.text: Do not try to learn all 165 points at once. Start with Parts 1 and 2 (rights and police), then traffic, cyber and money.
For any specific dispute, check the current law and take advice from a qualified lawyer. General information is a starting point, not a final answer.

practicalSteps: Bookmark the official websites and type the address yourself.
Keep your certificates, ID documents and receipts in one safe folder.
Raise local problems with your panchayat, municipality or ward office.
For any serious problem, get advice from a lawyer or free legal aid.
exceptions: RTI does not cover certain exempt matters, such as national security and personal privacy.
Some laws have been amended or replaced; always check the version that applies today.

faqs.q: Do I need to memorise all these laws?
faqs.a: No. Just know what each law is about. When you need it, look up the section or ask a lawyer.

faqs.q: Is the information here enough to win a case?
faqs.a: No. It helps you understand your position. For a real dispute, get a lawyer's advice.

misconceptions.myth: I must know every law to stay safe.
misconceptions.fact: No. Knowing a few key rights and habits covers most of daily life. Look up the rest when you need it.
